data.title: Prašník – Hrádok: a hillfort above the Lesser Carpathian pass
data.excerpt: The hillfort at Hrádok above the village of Prašník watched over the eastern mouth of the Lesser Carpathian pass and a long stretch of the road from Brezová pod Bradlom towards Vrbové. Occupied in turn by the Neolithic Ludanice group, the Maďarovce and Lusatian cultures, the Celts and finally the Slavs, it ended as a watch point that lost its purpose once the frontier of the Hungarian state shifted westwards.
data.metaTitle: Prašník – Hrádok: a Lesser Carpathian hillfort
data.metaDescription: The Hrádok hillfort near Prašník watched the eastern mouth of the Lesser Carpathian pass. It was occupied from the Neolithic to the Slavic period.

keyFacts.label: Strategic position
keyFacts.value: The promontory above the Holeška stream allowed control of a long stretch of the road from Brezová pod Bradlom towards Vrbové.

keyFacts.label: Height of the slope
keyFacts.value: The steep eastern face of the hillfort rises 110–117 m above the surrounding terrain.

keyFacts.label: Earliest occupation
keyFacts.value: The Ludanice group (a subgroup of the Lengyel culture), dated to c. 4400–4000 BC.

keyFacts.label: A Neolithic palisade
keyFacts.value: A palisade of hornbeam and oak trunks up to 25 cm in diameter was set into a foundation trench cut into the limestone rock.

keyFacts.label: The finest bronze find
keyFacts.value: A decorated axe-hammer with a long cylindrical socket, a chisel-like blade and a fan-shaped expanded butt, belonging to the Maďarovce culture.

keyFacts.label: Metal-casting workshop
keyFacts.value: A bronze-casting workshop of the Lusatian culture operated in the second enclosure – attested by a mould, a hoard of bronze rings and a freshly cast sickle.

keyFacts.label: A Slavic stone wall
keyFacts.value: The drystone wall originally stood at least three metres high; today it survives to a height of c. 150 cm.

children.text: The hillfort on the right-hand side of the eastern mouth of the Lesser Carpathian pass, at Hrádok in the cadastral area of the village of Prašník in the Trnava district, was sought out repeatedly despite the evidently unsuitable settlement conditions, thanks to a strategic position that allowed control of a fairly long stretch of the road from Brezová pod Bradlom further eastwards towards Vrbové. The route ran, and still runs today, along the Holeška stream at the northern foot of the promontory. From the first enclosure of the hillfort there was a very good view eastwards into the Trnava Hills, while from Dievčí vŕšok it was possible to watch travellers deep in the pass. As can be seen, the emphasis was on the ability to watch the road below the site along the longest possible stretch.
Štefan Janšák was the first to survey the hillfort, in the 1920s, that is, at a time when it had not yet been damaged by stone quarrying, and he described it as follows:

blocks.text: Hrádok extends on a tongue-shaped mountain promontory, connected in a north-westerly direction with a narrow ridge and ending to the south-east in a steep rock, or else a slope. Above the level of the high road the surface of the hrádok rises by 100 m, its highest points by 110 to 117 m. The north-eastern and eastern slope, as far as the 350 contour line, is covered with young beech wood; the south-western slope, as well as the surface of the hillfort, is pasture overgrown with shrubs that pass in places into dense, tall grass.

The rampart a b, 110 m long, closes off access to the hillfort from the ridge. The builders here made use of a very favourable natural swell of the ground, which they raised still further with an artificial rampart, so that even today spot height 367 rises a full 12 m above its surroundings, thus forming a secure obstacle. Running with rampart a b are two almost parallel ramparts, c d, 124 m long, and e f, 140 m long. Of these, rampart e f is of interest in that it rises on a natural step of the ground and attains a relative height of 10 m. On the south-western side runs the protective rampart a ce ei, 432 m long, interrupted by gate i, through which the hillfort was entered from the village of „Pustá Ves“ by the road y i. At the place ei g there is a precipitous slope, changing into the broken rock g h, which passes again into the precipitous slope h h\ f (dotted line). In the area ei g h h\ f d there is no artificial bank whatsoever. The boundary of the hillfort is determined here by the dotted line e\ g, h hl, by the rock g h and by the 350 contour line from point in as far as d. In the area d b there are low remains of ramparts, interrupted by the path k L By the transverse banks c d, e/ the surface of the hillfort is divided into three areas or enclosures: a c d b, c e f d, eei ghhif. Of these the first has an area of 1.33 ha, the second 3.15 ha, the third 2.6 ha. The entrenchments a b, c d, e f form a threefold protection against an enemy coming along the ridge, and the area e ei g h hi f may therefore be regarded as the core of the hrádok. Here, indeed, is the strongest occupation layer, sooty black humus, with the usual finds of pottery of the first Iron Age. The surface of the hillfort is inclined to the south-west, as can be seen from sections a–b, c–d, e–f, whereby the most favourable position towards the sun and against the northern winds is used. The protective rampart a c e e\ lies on average 20 m lower than the north-eastern edge of the hillfort b d f.

children.text: A modern and detailed excavation of the hillfort was carried out in the 1970s and 1980s by Petr Novák. He summarised his many years of research in a book published in
Bohemia
in 2011, because the West Slovak Museum, where he had submitted his manuscript as early as 2001, was not able (or not willing?) to publish it.

children.text: Novák states that on its western side the promontory of the hillfort merges with the massif of the Lesser Carpathians, while its steep eastern face rises 110–117 m above the surrounding terrain and is largely damaged by quarrying. Three belts of fortification cut across the promontory in a N–S direction, so that the western belt of fortification runs across „Dievčí Vŕšok“, which formed a natural swell of the ground separating the promontory from the ridge of the Lesser Carpathians. The belt of fortification set further to the east is built on the edge of a swell of the ground which is, however, not as pronounced as the break of slope that was used for the construction of the third belt of fortification, encircling the first enclosure. The area of the hillfort slopes to the south and along almost its whole length, with the exception of the rocky sections, it is lined by a belt of fortification linking all three enclosures.
The Neolithic

blocks.caption: Plan of the hillfort after Štefan Janšák
blocks.alt: Plan of the hillfort after Štefan Janšák

children.text: The earliest attested occupation of the site at Hrádok demonstrably belongs to the Ludanice group (a subgroup of the Lengyel culture dated to c. 4400–4000 BC), which is clearly documented by the pottery sherds found. Occupation in the Neolithic period is tied exclusively to the best-protected first enclosure of the hillfort. Beneath the main fortification on the edge of the swell of the ground between the first and the second enclosure, slight remains of architecture from this period have survived. Right on the edge delimiting the promontory, a palisade of hornbeam and oak trunks up to 25 cm in diameter was set into a foundation trench cut into the limestone bedrock. Not far from the palisade, remains of a post-built structure were found with a carefully plastered hearth floor. A violent end to the Ludanice occupation was not reflected in the finds, and everything suggests the site was simply abandoned at a time when the reasons for occupying strategically advantageous positions had passed.
Finds

Apart from poorly preserved pottery sherds, clay spindle whorls and bone awls and small chisels were found. Since we are in the Stone Age, ground stone axes, a scraper, an arrowhead and various small blades were found at the site, all of them of stone.
The Bronze Age
(The Maďarovce culture)

After a longer gap, already in the Early Bronze Age, the hilltop settlement was occupied by the people of the Maďarovce culture (before 1450 BC according to conventional dating, before 1600 BC according to more recent dating). The parts of vessels and other objects discovered have close analogies at several sites in western Slovakia, such as Veselé, Boleráz and Budmerice. Occupation was still confined only to the area of the first enclosure of the hillfort. On the levelled remains of the fortification of the Ludanice group, the newly arriving population of the Maďarovce culture first built a simple fence with widely spaced load-bearing posts about 2 m apart (probably interwoven with branches), and only afterwards replaced the makeshift enclosure with a rampart of heaped dolomite obtained by digging a ditch at the foot of the swell of the ground. The incohesive dolomite required consolidation with a grillage of transversely laid roundwood. Only on this base did a stone wall rise, the remains of which were found drawn back into the rear of the fortification during a further rebuilding of the main defences between the first and the second enclosure of the hillfort. Of the settlement features, only part of a larger rectangular building survived, with a carefully plastered floor on which a large amphora and a larger deep bowl stood in the south-western corner, with several sherds of another, smaller amphora lying beside them. The existence of the fortified Maďarovce hilltop settlement probably relates to the route below the northern foot of the promontory, and it could thus have served as a watch point on the link with the neighbouring Věteřov area. Traces of violent destruction, or more pronounced traces of a fire at the Maďarovce settlement at Hrádok, were not detected during the excavation.

children.text: Finds

Above all, the people of the Maďarovce culture left behind a varied range of pottery here, such as small jugs, cups, amphorae, bowls, pots and storage vessels. The finest bronze find is a decorated axe-hammer with a long cylindrical socket, a chisel-like blade and a fan-shaped expanded butt. Temple rings of double wire, a small bronze dagger and a heart-shaped pendant were also found.
(The Lusatian culture)

blocks.alt: Plan of the hillfort after Štefan Janšák

children.text: After a longer interval the site came to life again in the Final Bronze Age. The people of the Silesian phase of the Lusatian urnfields (around 1000 BC) renewed the main fortification of the first enclosure and extended the hillfort westwards by two further enclosures. The newly heaped ramparts cut across the natural elevation of Dievčí vŕšok at the point where it passes into the massif of the Lesser Carpathians and, carried on further eastwards, made access to the vulnerable southern side more difficult. The first enclosure served exclusively a settlement function, while in the south-western part of the second enclosure stood the production features of a metal-casting workshop. This is confirmed above all by a thin black layer with small droplets of bronze, a mould, a hoard of bronze rings and a freshly cast small sickle at the bottom of a settlement pit. Only a little to the east stood a hut with clay wedges which may have been used in casting bronze objects. The excavation did not fully clarify the role of the third enclosure, which probably served only as a connecting link on the elevation of Dievčí vŕšok. The inhabitants of the hillfort tried to overcome the lack of water by building a cistern on the north-eastern slope, which lay just above the working face of the quarry. In this period the hillfort served as a watch point above an important route between southern Moravia and the fertile Váh region. The occupation in the Final Bronze Age came to an end in an extensive fire. In the Early Iron Age (Hallstatt) the nearby hillfort of Tlstá hora was inhabited, which led me to speculate that it was precisely the people of the Hallstatt period who destroyed the hillfort u Fajnorov, but Dr Novák pointed out to me that this reasoning is wrong, because between the demise of the hillfort u Fajnorov and the emergence of the hillfort of Tlstá hora there is a gap of 150–200 years. The question of who destroyed the Lusatian hillfort therefore remains unanswered.
Finds

The Lusatian culture is known for very fine decorated pottery, and such pottery was found in larger quantities at Prašník as well. These are various cups, amphorae, small bowls, pots and storage vessels, and other vessels. Among the bronze objects found were above all pins, a „spectacle“ brooch with a figure-of-eight bow, a beautifully patinated torc, part of a belt mount, bracelets, finger rings, knives and arrowheads.
La Tène (the Late Iron Age)

For a short time the site came to life again in the La Tène period. The sherd material and the small objects found fall roughly into the period of the 2nd to 1st century BC, and they occur abundantly in western Slovakia. The hillfort apparently served as a stopping place for Celtic people on their march to the south-east, or as a watch point above the route. Novák interprets the hillfort in the La Tène period as a patrol point above one of the routes of the Celts' march eastwards.
The Slavs

The hillfort began to fulfil its purpose again only after the arrival of the Slavs, some time in the days of the Principality of Nitra, or at the beginnings of Great Moravia. The whole fortification system was gradually reconstructed, and two mutually unrelated interventions were apparent in the surviving architecture. The structurally accomplished wall probably relates to the earlier occupation, corresponding approximately to the finds from Pobedim. Without any firmer link to the preceding phase, the Slavic population later renewed the entire fortification once more, but the thorough constructions were replaced merely by heaped ramparts. On the southern side the Slavs added to the main wall of the first enclosure an arc-shaped rampart of loosely laid stone without mortar. At that time a row of partly sunken dwellings grew up along the ridge of the second enclosure of the hillfort.
Architecture

The newly built Slavic fortification made use of the remains of the earlier defensive system, above all that of the Final Bronze Age, when the fortified area reached its present extent and defined the basic lines. At the foot of the main rampart of the first enclosure, on the outer edge of the earlier ditch towards the second enclosure, a smaller rampart arose, and along its outer side a new V-shaped ditch was created. As for the main fortification, here a wall of drystone-laid stone is built on carefully levelled bedrock. The height of the rampart surviving today reaches c. 150 cm and a thickness of approximately 120–130 cm. Judging by the quantity of stone found on the western slope and at its foot, the original wall was at least three metres high. Drystone-laid stone did not guarantee sufficient strength for the wall, and therefore vertical beams were erected in front of its face, fixed with roundwood inserted transversely into the stone wall. Behind them, during the construction, thinner longitudinal oak trunks were inserted, which together with the stones formed the facing of the wall. In a certain sense, timber chamber structures with a stone outer wall were thus created. Far less attention was devoted to the fortification of the second and third enclosures. Heaped ramparts with a stone facing were identified along the southern side of the hillfort, and also in the fortification between the second and the third enclosure. The existence of an arc-shaped rampart attached on the southern side to the main fortification of the first enclosure was also established, which Novák likewise attributes to the Slavic period.

The semi-sunken buildings typical of the Slavic period could be identified only in the second enclosure of the hillfort, whereas in the first enclosure traces of domestic architecture are entirely absent. This may be due partly to a different character of building, with only ground-level structures standing in the area of the first enclosure, and partly to the very hard rocky bedrock, which made the sinking of a semi-sunken building impossible. Stone hearths were identified in most of the semi-sunken buildings in the second enclosure. In one hut an undamaged covered stone hearth was found, still with remains of ash. From the original furnishings of one hut comes a reconstructed, unusually large vessel, which the owner of the dwelling threw away on leaving the site in such a way that the sherds from its base lay close to the hearth while the rim parts were found in the opposite corner. The large dimensions of some Slavic pots may be connected with the distant source of water in the Holeška river, from which they were separated by a height difference of about 110 m. In times of drought, when the cistern dried up, the little river below the northern slope of the hillfort was the only source of water. As in the case of the earlier occupations of the site, storage pits that would have allowed longer-term storage of grain are again entirely absent, and the livelihood of the inhabitants therefore depended on supplies from the hinterland of the hillfort. In its immediate surroundings, surveys have not demonstrated traces of a lowland agricultural settlement, and so the Slavic population evidently had to bring food in from a greater distance.
Finds

The pottery is almost exclusively confined to classic pots, known from many other Slavic sites and decorated with the typical wavy line. Among the metal objects, a finger ring of thin bronze sheet from the middle of the 9th century was found, together with an iron spade shoe, seven iron knives, arrowheads, an iron fire-steel with curved arms, a broken iron belt with narrowed ends, an iron mount, part of a small iron axe, two forged nails, an axe-shaped currency bar with a rectangular hole in its butt and an iron awl. Several bone objects, a glass bead and part of a quernstone were also found.

The earlier Slavic occupation might perhaps be connected with the period of the Principality of Nitra (links to the important hillfort of Pobedim), when it guarded the traffic on the road leading into the Nitra region. The demise of the first phase of Slavic occupation of the hillfort at Hrádok may equally well be connected with the fate of Pobedim. This is the period of the incorporation of the Principality of Nitra into Great Moravia. The carefully built earlier fortification and finds very similar to objects from Staré Město would argue for relations with Great Moravia. Further settlement phases might perhaps be connected with the penetration of the Old Hungarians into the territory of present-day Slovakia, when hillforts were very important to the Slavs for reasons of defence. In the case of the later Slavic occupation, the construction of the ramparts differs entirely from the earlier phase and nothing suggests that there was any continuity or connection. At that time the arc-shaped rampart adjoining the outer edge of the main fortification of the first enclosure was also created, and in the second enclosure a row of dwellings grew up along the ridge. Novák states that in the times after the fall of Great Moravia the hillfort might have had a connection with the campaigns of Boleslav I in western Slovakia. Once conditions in the Hungarian state had stabilised, the hillfort lost its purpose, because the frontier shifted westwards and the population could descend from the hills into the area of the present-day little town of Vrbové, which lies in a substantially more favourable natural environment.
Present state and signage:

The hillfort has been damaged by the quarry, but the greater part of it survives to this day. We got to spot height 382 (Hrádok) along the blue trail (a steep climb) and then along the ridge you come right up to the quarry. The hillfort is not marked in any way whatsoever; of an information panel there is not the faintest sign. In this respect, 0 points. If you visit with children, be on your guard, because the quarry faces are high and there are no barriers or warnings there.
